items.abstract: <jats:p>Algorithmic decision-making systems now shape hiring, lending, health care, policing, education, and the flow of information online. Concerns about "algorithmic bias" have grown accordingly, but relevant research often remains siloed: social psychologists study categorization, stereotypes, and discrimination, while computer scientists study biased data, biased models, and formal fairness criteria. This chapter bridges the two literatures by treating algorithmic systems as artifacts of social cognition: the targets algorithms learn to predict are frequently the product of human judgments; models learn statistical regularities that mirror those judgments; and people then interpret and act on model outputs in discretionary ways. We organize this argument using the Algorithmic Cognition Cycle, a framework that traces bias across three linked stages-(1) biased human judgments and records (data generation), (2) bias in data representations and model predictions (model training), and (3) bias in how humans deploy, trust, and override algorithmic advice (human-algorithm decision making)-with feedback loops that can amplify disparities over time. Along the way we pair classic psychological mechanisms (e.g., social identity, stereotype content, motivated reasoning) with computational analogs (e.g., proxy labels, embeddings, fairness metrics, explainability tools), highlight limits of "purely technical" fixes in a persistently biased world, and offer actionable intervention points spanning data, models, interfaces, and governance. The goal is a shared vocabulary and a research roadmap that is maximally useful to graduate students working at the intersection of psychology and computer science.</jats:p>
